Researchers studying the Omei whipping frog (Zhangixalus omeimontis) have documented key size benchmarks across its life cycle. At the completion of larval metamorphosis, the snout-vent length of recently metamorphosed froglets averages about 1.8 cm , a value that marks the transition from an aquatic tadpole to a terrestrial juvenile. This relatively modest size at metamorphosis is typical for rhacophorid frogs of this genus. Following the juvenile phase, the attainment of sexual maturity, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation and the ability to produce gametes, occurs when individuals reach a snout-vent length of approximately 5.5 cm [Lp = approximately 5.5 cm]. This measurement serves as a critical threshold, separating the pre-reproductive sub-adult stage from reproductively viable adults. Body size at first reproduction is a pivotal life-history trait often linked to local resource availability and population density, and this species appears to follow a pattern comparable to other montane anurans that allocate substantial growth to the juvenile period before maturing.

Information on the ultimate maximum body size attained by adult individuals of Zhangixalus omeimontis reveals notable variation between sexes. Most field surveys report that the largest adult females reach a maximum snout-vent length of 7 cm [Li = 7 cm] under typical montane forest conditions. However, particularly fecund or old individuals, especially those from lower-elevation populations with extended growing seasons, have been recorded achieving a snout-vent length as high as 8.5 cm [Li = 8.5 cm]. This larger size represents the upper boundary of ultimate body size documented for the species. Corresponding with this skeletal dimension, the maximum adult wet weight recorded for these large females is approximately 23.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 23.6 grams]. This estimate is derived from predictive length-weight regressions calibrated on data from related treefrog species, which account for the cubic relationship between linear growth and volumetric mass gain. Such a substantive adult body mass, nearly an order of magnitude greater than the mass at birth, underscores the considerable somatic investment required during the post-metamorphic growth phase.

Reproductive output in Zhangixalus omeimontis has been characterized through field observations of gravid females and their foam nests. During the breeding season, a single clutch typically contains between 457 and 837 eggs [N_R_i = single clutch typically contains between 457 and 837 eggs], a range that reflects variability associated with female body size and age. Each female produces only one such clutch per season [F_R_i = one such clutch per season], a reproductive frequency that aligns with the species' high-elevation habitat where the active period is constrained by cooler temperatures. The annual reproductive effort is therefore concentrated into a single, large spawning event. The construction of a foam nest is energetically demanding, and the relatively fixed, single clutch per season suggests a strategy wherein females invest heavily in a single cohort of offspring rather than spreading reproductive effort across multiple smaller clutches. At a controlled experimental temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the physiological capacity underlying this reproductive schedule translates to a daily production rate consistent with the annual total, though in natural conditions temperature fluctuations modulate actual egg development rates.

Early-life development in Z. omeimontis is characterized by specific thermal dependencies that govern embryonic and larval duration. Embryonated eggs, which are deposited within a gelatinous foam nest that protects them from desiccation and pathogens, undergo rapid development. The age at birth, defined as the time from egg deposition to larval eclosion from the jelly capsule, is approximately 13.9 days [ab = approximately 13.9 days] when incubated at a constant temperature of 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C]. This relatively short incubation period, even at the cool temperatures typical of the species' montane breeding ponds, allows the synchrony of hatching with optimal conditions for the free-swimming tadpole stage. At the moment of hatching, the emergent larvae are still dependent on yolk reserves. Their wet weight at birth is very slight, measuring only about 0.0172 grams [Wwb = about 0.0172 grams]. This minute mass, characteristic of the small egg diameter of approximately 2.9 to 3.4 mm, reflects the limited endogenous resources available to the endotrophic larva before it must commence exogenous filter feeding on suspended organic particles and algae.

Longevity data for the Omei whipping frog in its natural habitat remain sparse, but estimates derived from mark-recapture studies of related species suggest that the maximum lifespan of Zhangixalus omeimontis is approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] under field conditions, a figure based on the demography of the European treefrog Hyla arborea, which occupies a similar ec at a temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C]ological niche. This estimate, considered valid for a constant ambient temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C], positions the species within the moderate longevity range typical for small-bodied anurans that experience seasonal dormancy. The six-year maximum likely applies only to individuals that successfully avoid predation, disease, and habitat disturbance across multiple breeding seasons.
